strengths: Addresses a practical and previously underexplored problem in generalizable 3D reconstruction—handling transient distractors in unconstrained real-world scenes with clear motivation
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple real and synthetic datasets (On-the-go, RobusNeRF, Re10K, ACID) with thorough ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution
Sound technical approach combining reference-based mask prediction, mask refinement, and two-stage inference with clear improvements over baselines (PSNR: 21.02 vs 19.45)
Strong reproducibility commitment with promise to release code and detailed experimental setup including training/evaluation protocols
Clear visual presentation of problem, method, and results with effective figures demonstrating distractor removal capability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—individual components (consistency-based mask prediction, entity segmentation, reference selection) are relatively standard techniques, with the contribution feeling more like an engineering solution than a fundamental advance
Dense presentation with heavy mathematical notation that obscures intuition; key concepts like why loss-based detection identifies distractors lack clear explanation before formal definitions

Insufficient theoretical justification—the core assumption that 'high-loss regions correspond to distractors' is not rigorously validated, and there is no analysis of when/why the approach succeeds or fails

Experimental fairness concerns—comparison with scene-specific methods using per-scene optimization is not directly comparable to generalizable methods; hyperparameter sensitivity (ρ₁, ρ₂, K) is underexplored and no statistical significance testing is provided

Practical limitations inadequately addressed: method requires paired references (what if all contain distractors?), fixed K=4 references, dependence on SAM for segmentation, and unclear generalization beyond 3DGS; efficiency trade-off (Table 5) mentioned but not discussed

Important implementation details missing from main text and appendix: scene-images pool construction, reference scorer architecture, exact loss combinations, and initialization procedures remain unclear

Fixed hyperparameters (ρ₁, ρ₂) applied across diverse scenes lacks adaptability; unclear how method handles scenarios where distractors appear in most reference views

Comprehensive experimental validation on multiple real and synthetic datasets (On-the-go, RobustNeRF, Re10K, ACID) with consistent improvements (PSNR 21.02 vs 19.45-19.29 for baselines)
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-4) demonstrating the contribution of each component and supporting design choices
Clear presentation with well-designed figures effectively illustrating the pipeline and results; commitment to code release supports reproducibility
Practical relevance: directly addresses constraints that practitioners face in generalizable 3DGS for out-of-the-box capture scenarios
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (reference-based prediction, entity segmentation, pruning) in a relatively straightforward manner without significant algorithmic innovation
Heuristic design choices lack strong justification: mask intersection operation (Eq. 6), simple pixel-wise reference scoring (Eq. 10), and fixed hyperparameters (ρ₁, ρ₂) appear ad-hoc
Efficiency concerns not adequately addressed: Table 5 shows decreased efficiency (0.880 vs 0.904 fps) compared to baseline; no detailed runtime/memory analysis or scalability discussion
Incomplete experimental analysis: missing statistical significance testing, limited parameter sensitivity analysis, no systematic study of performance degradation with distractor density

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and limitations: limited discussion of when/why reference scoring fails, which distractor types are handled poorly, or how method degrades under extensive occlusions
Reliance on pre-trained entity segmentation model as potential bottleneck: no analysis of sensitivity to segmentation quality or applicability to novel distractor types
Narrow problem scope specific to 3DGS generalization with limited broader applicability; impact likely confined to specialized view synthesis subcommunity

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: Addresses a genuine challenge in generalizable 3DGS with distractors, which is important for real-world applications
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive experiments across multiple datasets (On-the-go, RobustNeRF, synthetic) with numerous baselines and thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-6)
Clear methodology and structure: Two-stage approach (training paradigm and inference framework) is logically motivated and well-organized
Strong qualitative results: Figures 5, 7, and 14-15 demonstrate clear visual improvements handling complex real-world scenes with distractors
Reproducibility commitment: Detailed experimental settings in appendices, promised code release, and clear implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contributions are primarily engineering-focused, combining existing techniques (reference-based masking, pre-trained segmentation models, distractor pruning) without fundamental new insights or methods
Marginal empirical improvements: DGGS-TR achieves ~2% PSNR improvement over baselines (21.02 vs. 20.60), which may not justify added complexity; no statistical significance testing provided

Heavy underexplored dependence on reference frames: Method requires N=4 references from query scenes for both training and inference, significantly constraining true generalizability; ablation on N (Fig. 10) is minimal with only 2-3 data points

Critical reliance on external segmentation without proper analysis: Performance depends heavily on Entity Segmentation (Qi et al., 2022) quality, but propagation of segmentation errors is not analyzed; failure cases (Fig. 16) show masks still problematic

Overstated generalizability claim: While marketed as 'generalizable,' the requirement for scene-specific reference frames effectively makes this semi-supervised; true applicability depends on reference availability
Low resolution experiments: All experiments use 192×256 resolution (quite low by modern standards), reducing benchmark competitiveness and practical relevance

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Most compared methods are scene-specific rather than other generalizable approaches; limited comparison with concurrent work (Chen et al., 2024a; Ungermann et al., 2024); no significance testing

Shallow ablation studies: Table 2 lacks detail on ablating components; no analysis of reference scoring mechanism effectiveness or mask fusion strategy alternatives; limited study of hyperparameter sensitivity (K, N, τ)
Efficiency trade-offs underexplored: Two-stage inference increases computational cost; segmentation model inference overhead during training/inference not thoroughly analyzed relative to baseline

Clarity issues in presentation: Distinction between DGGS-TR and DGGS unclear early; dense mathematical formulation (Eqs. 1-9) obscures intuition; some design choices lack justification (e.g., why intersection for mask fusion in Eq. 5?)
Limited failure analysis: Figure 16 shows failures superficially; systematic analysis of when/why method fails is missing; no quantitative evaluation of failure frequency or types
Weak generalization validation: Method doesn't work without references; true novel scene generalization not adequately demonstrated; evaluation uses 'extra' views from same dataset

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical problem in real-world 3D reconstruction that existing generalizable 3DGS methods struggle with
Well-designed reference-based framework that coherently integrates mask prediction, refinement, reference scoring, and distractor pruning into a unified system
Comprehensive experimental validation with extensive ablation studies (Tables 1-13), comparisons on both real and synthetic datasets, and both quantitative and qualitative results
Demonstrates significant performance improvements (PSNR: 21.02 vs. 15.45 on RobustNeRF) and good generalization compared to scene-specific distractor-free methods
Clear presentation with informative figures and detailed implementation information; authors commit to code release for reproducibility
Clever use of 3D consistency across reference images to infer distractor masks without explicit per-scene supervision
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty - combines relatively standard techniques (reference-based segmentation, mask refinement, reference selection) rather than introducing conceptually new ideas
Weak theoretical justification for why 3D consistency should reliably identify distractors; transient objects may still exhibit 3D structure across views, and the assumption lacks rigorous analysis
Efficiency trade-offs not adequately addressed; inference time increases significantly (20.9s vs. 11.1s) but computational overhead is not thoroughly analyzed or justified
Experimental design concerns: uses additional synthetic data (COCO masks) providing unfair comparison advantages; pre-trained models potentially benefit from domain similarity to test scenes
Limited generalization validation - primarily evaluated on indoor RobustNeRF scenes and specific outdoor contexts; unclear performance on extremely crowded scenes or very different environments

Technical clarity issues: complex formulations (e.g., Eq. 4) with inconsistent notation; the distractor pruning strategy is vaguely described; conservative mask fusion strategy may miss distractors but trade-offs unexplored
Incomplete analysis of sensitivity to hyperparameters, reference image quality effects, and failure modes beyond the limited examples shown in Figure 16
